story.headline: North Korea expels Swiss envoy, shuts office
story.summary: North Korea declared the head of the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang persona non grata and demanded the office close over Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon camp.
story.display_body: North Korea has declared Sylvain Astier, head of the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang, persona non grata and given him 48 hours to leave, the state agency KCNA reported on Wednesday 25 November. According to KCNA, Pak Hyon Su, director-general for Europe at the North Korean foreign ministry, summoned Astier and handed him a memorandum demanding that the office close. KCNA called Switzerland's sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp near Wonsan a "hostile act". The day before, Kim Yo Jong had threatened to close the office over the same sanctions. Switzerland imposed them in early November when it adopted the EU's 21st Russia package, which targets the camp for taking part in programmes that bring Ukrainian children from occupied territories there. The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) had said on Tuesday that neither the Swiss embassy in Beijing nor the Pyongyang office had been officially contacted. It said its sanctions policy is separate from its diplomatic presence and that the office exists to keep channels of dialogue open. The office only reopened on 19 October, after Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis visited Pyongyang.
story.why: barely five weeks after it reopened, Switzerland is about to lose one of the few Western channels into Pyongyang, because it adopted EU sanctions.

story.headline: Pregnancy care free of cost-sharing from day one
story.summary: From 1 January 2027 pregnant women are exempt from deductible and co-payment from the start of pregnancy, pharmacists can bill vaccinations, and out-of-canton reference tariffs are harmonised.
story.display_body: From 1 January 2027, pregnant women will pay no deductible or co-payment from the first day of pregnancy instead of from the 13th week, the Federal Council decided on Wednesday 25 November. The change is one of several measures from parliament's second cost-containment package of March 2025 that the government is now bringing into force. From the same date, midwives as well as doctors can notify the insurer that a pregnancy has begun. Pharmacists will be able to bill basic health insurance for helping patients take their medicines correctly and for certain prevention services, and to give some vaccines, including the flu jab, to people aged 16 and over without a prescription. Cantons must also change how they set "reference tariffs", the most that basic insurance pays when a patient is treated in a hospital outside their home canton. By 1 January 2029 at the latest, these must match the highest tariff for a comparable treatment in a hospital on the home canton's list, so choosing a hospital elsewhere should no longer leave patients with extra costs. The communiqué does not estimate what the measures will cost or save.
story.why: early pregnancy is when costs often land on the deductible, and a flu jab at the pharmacy paid by basic insurance changes everyday access to care from January.

story.headline: Bern proposes one flat work-expense deduction
story.summary: The Federal Council adopted a bill replacing itemised work-expense deductions, including meals, with a single flat deduction while keeping commuting deductions separate.
story.display_body: The Federal Council sent parliament a bill on Wednesday 25 November that would replace most itemised work-expense tax deductions for employees with a single flat deduction. Commuting costs and the cost of staying away from home during the week would still be deducted separately. Everything else, including meals eaten away from home, would go into one flat amount that needs no receipts, is the same whether people work at home or in the office, and is reduced only for those who work part of the year. Taxpayers could no longer deduct their actual costs instead. The Finance Department would set the federal amount so that the reform costs the federal budget as little as possible, and each canton would set its own amount. The government had wanted to fold commuting costs into the flat deduction too, but dropped this after most cantons opposed it in consultation.
story.why: everyone who works from home gains the meal allowance, but anyone whose actual work costs are higher than the flat amount loses the right to claim them. Parliament now decides.

story.headline: Solar subsidies rise from January
story.summary: The Federal Council raised one-off payments for small and mid-sized photovoltaic installations and revised several energy ordinances effective 1 January 2027.
story.display_body: The Federal Council raised the one-off subsidy for small and mid-sized solar installations on Wednesday 25 November, as part of a set of revised energy ordinances that take effect on 1 January 2027. The capacity-based payment rises by CHF 40 per kilowatt both for installations under 30 kW and for those from 30 to 100 kW. The higher one-off payment for installations under 150 kW that do not use their own power is now CHF 550 per kW. The same package cuts investment grants for biomass plants while raising their operating grants, ends federal support for solar thermal heat for industry, and simplifies planning for high-voltage lines, so that the government sets the route corridor and the choice between overhead line and cable directly. It also changes how nuclear operators' contribution to federal liability cover is calculated.

story.headline: Non-EU work permit quotas held for 2027
story.summary: The Federal Council kept 2027 quotas for third-country skilled workers at 8,500 and left EU/EFTA service-provider and UK quotas unchanged.
story.display_body: The Federal Council kept quotas for skilled workers from outside the EU and EFTA (the European Free Trade Association) unchanged for 2027, at 8,500 permits, on Wednesday 25 November. That is 4,500 residence (B) permits and 4,000 short-term (L) permits. The 3,500 permits for EU/EFTA service providers working in Switzerland more than 120 days a year and the 3,500 for UK citizens also stay the same. Companies used only 69% of the third-country quota in 2025, down from 74% a year earlier. The government pointed to an unemployment rate of 3% in September 2026, up 0.2 points on a year earlier.

story.headline: EFTA–Thailand trade deal starts in January
story.summary: The EFTA–Thailand free trade agreement enters into force on 1 January 2027, giving tariff relief to 99.7% of current Swiss exports to Thailand.
story.display_body: The free trade agreement between the EFTA states and Thailand will take effect on 1 January 2027, the Federal Council said on Wednesday 25 November. It adopted the ordinance changes needed to apply the agreed tariff cuts. Bern says 99.7% of current Swiss exports to Thailand will get tariff relief, some only after transition periods. Trade in goods between the two countries, excluding precious metals, was about CHF 2 billion in 2025. The deal was signed in Davos on 23 January 2025 and approved by parliament on 20 March 2026.

story.headline: Rights court sets rules for weaponised migration
story.summary: The ECHR Grand Chamber ruled that removals to an instrumentalising state are not in themselves an Article 3 violation but states must identify vulnerable people first.
story.display_body: The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday 24 November that when a hostile state deliberately sends migrants across a border, returning them to that state is not in itself a violation of the ban on inhuman treatment, but border authorities must first identify people who are especially at risk. The three cases involved Afghans, Iraqi Kurds and Cubans who tried to enter Poland, Latvia and Lithuania from Belarus in 2021–22. The court used the term "instrumentalisation of migration" for this tactic of pushing migrants towards a neighbour's border to destabilise it. It said states may restrict entry or even close their borders entirely, and that they need not check whether migrants would have access to asylum in Belarus. Before returning anyone, however, they must screen for two groups: people with evident vulnerabilities (age, illness, disability) and people with a specific basis to claim a real and immediate risk of ill-treatment. The court unanimously found violations for one Afghan applicant whom Poland removed to Belarus on 20 October 2021 despite an interim court order, and for the children and their accompanying families in the Latvian case. It found no violation for the Latvian adults and, by 11 votes to 6, none in the Lithuanian case.
story.why: this is the first time Europe's top human-rights court has set out the rules for "weaponised" migration, and the standard applies in all 46 Council of Europe states, Switzerland among them.

story.headline: Reports: Russian nuclear satellite within months
story.summary: German media citing Western intelligence report that Russia could put a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within two months; Paris deems the risk serious and the Kremlin dismisses it.
story.display_body: Several German media outlets reported on Tuesday 24 November that Western intelligence believes Russia could place a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead in orbit within about two months. Le Monde reports that Paris considers the risk serious. Citing work by intelligence services and Western military officials, including Germany's armed forces and its foreign intelligence agency (BND), the reports say the satellite, named "Sputnik-S", has already been built and is stored near Moscow. The outlets did not name specific sources. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that because of this it was "hardly worth taking them seriously". Washington has warned since 2024 that Moscow is working on such a weapon. What is new is the reported launch timeline. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which Russia has signed, bans placing nuclear weapons in orbit. Antje Nötzold, a space-security researcher at the Bundeswehr University Munich, told SRF that a nuclear explosion in orbit would immediately destroy nearby satellites and leave radiation that could disable others for months, cutting off satellite communications and the positioning and timing signals that transport, power grids and payments rely on.
story.why: the claim is unconfirmed and comes from anonymous sourcing, but it is the first reported date for a move that would break a 60-year ban on nuclear weapons in orbit.

story.headline: Houthi drones target Saudi oil terminal
story.summary: Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi drones over Ras Tanura after a Houthi drone struck Riyadh's tallest tower, injuring 11.
story.display_body: Saudi air defences destroyed four Houthi drones over the Ras Tanura oil refinery and export terminal on Wednesday 25 November, the day after a Houthi drone hit Riyadh's tallest tower and injured 11 people, Saudi officials said. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said falling fragments caused no casualties in an initial assessment. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the strikes on Ras Tanura had started fires, and that a three-phase attack had hit Riyadh's financial district. The tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was first struck on Thursday 19 November. Tuesday's attack followed coalition air strikes on the Red Sea port of Hodeidah, the main entry point for food into Houthi-held northern Yemen. The Houthis told workers and residents near Saudi Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, to evacuate. Qatar and Pakistan, which are mediating between Iran and the United States, condemned the strike on the tower.

story.headline: US jury convicts Huawei on sanctions, theft
story.summary: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries of Iran sanctions violations, bank fraud, money laundering and trade-secret conspiracy.
story.display_body: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei and three of its subsidiaries on Tuesday 24 November of violating US sanctions on Iran, bank fraud, money laundering and conspiring to steal trade secrets, after a three-month trial. DW reports that the jury found the company guilty on 10 of 12 counts and acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy and of conspiring to obstruct justice. According to the Justice Department, Huawei ran its Iran business through a subsidiary called Skycom, which it falsely described to banks as an independent partner, and supplied Iran with network infrastructure and with tools to monitor and censor internet users. The department said the victims of the trade-secret thefts included Cisco, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile and Fujitsu. These are the prosecution's descriptions of what was proven at trial. No sentence has been set, and Huawei's response was not available.

story.headline: EPFL theory predicts fusion's H-mode power threshold
story.summary: Tokamaks hold a plasma (a gas so hot its electrons are stripped off) inside a doughnut-shaped magnetic cage
story.display_body: Tokamaks hold a plasma (a gas so hot its electrons are stripped off) inside a doughnut-shaped magnetic cage. Since 1982 experimenters have known that above a certain heating power the plasma abruptly enters "H-mode" (high confinement): turbulence at the edge collapses and heat stays in far better. ITER and every planned power plant depend on it, but the threshold power has so far been predicted only from empirical fits to past machines, and no theory explained together why it first falls and then rises with plasma density and why it depends on the magnetic field's direction. The Swiss Plasma Center team ran flux-driven two-fluid simulations of a tokamak edge, partly on the Daint supercomputer at CSCS in Lugano. They show that the turbulence itself generates sheared flows — neighbouring layers of plasma moving at different speeds — that tear the eddies apart. The field-direction asymmetry, reproduced in simulation for the first time, arises because collisions between particles break the time-reversal symmetry of the problem. From this they derive scaling laws for the power threshold in both the high- and low-density branches, matching or beating the accuracy of the existing empirical scalings. Applied to machines under construction, the model predicts ITER needs at least 43 MW of heating against the 73 MW it will have, but that Commonwealth Fusion Systems' compact SPARC needs about 26 MW against a planned 25 MW.
story.why: a threshold derived from physics is something reactor designers can extrapolate to machines that do not exist yet, which an empirical fit cannot safely do. The work is Swiss-funded (SNSF, SERI) and EUROfusion-funded, and the SPARC figure is a prediction that operating that machine will test.

story.headline: Quantum chip wins games classical players cannot
story.summary: Contextuality is a basic quantum property: a measurement's outcome cannot be fixed in advance independently of which other compatible measurements are made alongside it
story.display_body: Contextuality is a basic quantum property: a measurement's outcome cannot be fixed in advance independently of which other compatible measurements are made alongside it. It can be tested with cooperative games in which players who cannot communicate must give answers satisfying a joint rule. In the "magic square" game the best classical strategy wins at most 8 of 9 rounds, while players sharing entangled qubits can in principle always win. On a superconducting processor the team plays that game with a few qubits and quantifies the effect through a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality violation (a numerical test that rules out pre-assigned answers). It then scales up to the N-player GHZ game and to a two-dimensional hidden-linear-function problem, which shallow quantum circuits provably solve better than shallow classical ones, reporting the best fidelity and system size so far on both. Unlike random-circuit "quantum advantage" claims, these separations rest on proofs rather than on how hard a task is to simulate today. The tasks themselves have no practical use.
story.why: it gives a way to benchmark quantum processors whose pass mark comes from a theorem, so a faster classical algorithm later cannot retroactively overturn the result.

story.headline: Dipolar excitons form a lattice supersolid
story.summary: A supersolid is a paradoxical state that is crystalline — its particles sit in a regular, symmetry-breaking pattern — and superfluid, flowing without friction, at the same time
story.display_body: A supersolid is a paradoxical state that is crystalline — its particles sit in a regular, symmetry-breaking pattern — and superfluid, flowing without friction, at the same time. Until now the evidence came from a few ultracold atomic gases in the weakly interacting regime. This French–Italian–US team uses dipolar excitons, bound electron–hole pairs in semiconductor layers that behave like tiny electrical bar magnets, confined in an artificial lattice in which they can hop over long distances. At one-quarter, one-third and one-half filling of the lattice sites, the excitons form crystals spanning about 100 sites that spontaneously break the lattice's translational symmetry. Simultaneously the long-range hopping keeps them phase-coherent across the sample, the signature of superfluid order. Numerical simulations of the lattice model confirm that supersolidity is a property of its ground state. The crystals are mesoscopic rather than bulk.
story.why: it moves supersolids out of the fragile weak-interaction corner into the strongly interacting regime, on a solid-state platform that can be tuned electrically.

story.headline: Ethiopian volcano vented a record methane outburst
story.summary: Volcanoes normally emit carbon dioxide and very little methane, so geologists have lacked modern analogues for magma cooking methane out of buried sediments — a process linked to abrupt climate shifts in Earth's deep past
story.display_body: Volcanoes normally emit carbon dioxide and very little methane, so geologists have lacked modern analogues for magma cooking methane out of buried sediments — a process linked to abrupt climate shifts in Earth's deep past. After a mega-dyke intrusion in 2025 (molten rock forcing its way through a crack underground), Fentale volcano in Ethiopia's East African Rift never erupted, but satellites measured at least 38.2 ± 3.9 thousand tonnes of methane released over three months, plus at least 2.9 ± 1.0 million tonnes of CO₂. The peak methane rate, 157 ± 41 tonnes an hour, is comparable to a major industrial gas blowout and roughly four orders of magnitude above other volcanic systems. The emissions coincided with localised ground subsidence and thermal anomalies inside the caldera. The authors propose that the intrusion broke an impermeable cap over methane generated from hydrocarbon-rich sediments. They are explicit that one outburst is small next to annual natural and human emissions.
story.why: it identifies an unrecognised source of episodic methane, and gives climate scientists a modern, measurable version of a process they have only been able to infer from the rock record.

story.headline: Chemists program fully substituted benzene rings
story.summary: The benzene ring is the most common ring system in small-molecule drugs, but rings carrying six substituents are almost absent from screening libraries, because making them with control over which group goes where is hard and the building blocks are not sold
story.display_body: The benzene ring is the most common ring system in small-molecule drugs, but rings carrying six substituents are almost absent from screening libraries, because making them with control over which group goes where is hard and the building blocks are not sold. The Tarragona-led team assembles them from aromatic cyclopropenium cations (positively charged three-carbon rings) and silyl-substituted allenes, with all six positions encoded in the starting materials. Density-functional calculations trace the near-perfect selectivity to an unusual "non-classical" carbocation intermediate in which four atoms share four electrons. They use the reaction to make previously inaccessible five- and six-substituted analogues of the cancer drug sonidegib and the blood-pressure drug telmisartan, and show that starting from a single-handed allene preserves that handedness in the product.
story.why: it opens a region of drug-like chemical space that medicinal chemists have mostly been unable to enter.

story.headline: Wernicke's area holds a word-planning subzone
story.summary: Textbooks call Wernicke's area, in the left temporal lobe, the brain's speech-comprehension centre, yet damage there also badly disrupts speaking — a paradox as old as the diagnosis
story.display_body: Textbooks call Wernicke's area, in the left temporal lobe, the brain's speech-comprehension centre, yet damage there also badly disrupts speaking — a paradox as old as the diagnosis. Using recordings from electrode grids placed on patients' brains during clinical monitoring, direct cortical stimulation and lesion analysis, the UCSF team isolates a distinct subzone, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus. It becomes active before speech begins, and interfering with it impairs production, so it is causally necessary rather than merely correlated. Its activity encodes features of whole upcoming words, not the sounds of them or the mouth movements needed to say them, and it is distinct from the neighbouring responses to hearing one's own voice. The same signal could be used to decode intended speech in people with paralysis. The participants are a small, clinically specific group.
story.why: it resolves a long-standing puzzle about aphasia (loss of language after brain injury), and identifies a word-level signal that speech neuroprostheses could read.

story.headline: Undergraduates led COVID variant spread
story.summary: The team linked more than 85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected in Massachusetts between November 2021 and January 2023 to epidemiological records from 666 settings, including schools, colleges and skilled nursing facilities
story.display_body: The team linked more than 85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected in Massachusetts between November 2021 and January 2023 to epidemiological records from 666 settings, including schools, colleges and skilled nursing facilities. Genome sequences trace who infected whom far better than case counts do. Elevated transmission turned out to be concentrated in three age-defined groups — older adolescents in schools, undergraduates in colleges and residents of nursing facilities — with little extra risk for other people in the same buildings, staff included. Young adults in colleges played a disproportionate role, and new viral lineages consistently expanded there first before spreading more widely. Spread followed a repeatable urban-to-rural gradient, and vaccination was associated with less onward transmission. The authors also estimate how much sequencing is needed to catch an emerging variant in time. This is one US state during the Omicron era, and the findings are observational associations.
story.why: it says where to put genomic surveillance for the earliest warning of the next respiratory-virus variant, and which settings generated risk rather than merely recording cases.

story.headline: EPFL finds second guard on ancient viral DNA
story.summary: At least a quarter of the sequences that regulate human genes are derived from transposable elements — mobile pieces of DNA, many of them descended from ancient viruses, that have accumulated over millions of years
story.display_body: At least a quarter of the sequences that regulate human genes are derived from transposable elements — mobile pieces of DNA, many of them descended from ancient viruses, that have accumulated over millions of years. They are a source of new genetic switches, but uncontrolled they can wreck a cell, so the genome keeps most of them shut. The known mechanism uses KRAB zinc-finger proteins, which recruit machinery that marks the proteins DNA wraps around and locks the region into a closed state. Only a small fraction of transposable elements are covered this way. Didier Trono's lab at EPFL, with postdoc Wayo Matsushima, traced a second family — SCAN zinc-finger proteins, whose defining domain itself originated as a captured retroviral capsid gene — across 68 vertebrate genomes, and found it expanded independently in different animal lineages, with each protein recognising elements of a matching evolutionary age. Mapping their binding sites in human cells showed these proteins work without the usual chemical silencing marks: the DNA is simply kept inaccessible, and resists being pried open even by "pioneer" factors such as SOX2 and OCT4. Remove one of the proteins for a few hours and the region opens; put it back and it closes again.
story.why: it describes a distinct, more local way cells keep inherited viral DNA quiet while still allowing it to supply new regulatory switches over evolutionary time — one of the mechanisms that makes species differ in how their genes are controlled.

story.headline: Euclid finds first quasar beyond redshift 8
story.summary: A quasar is a galaxy's core blazing as gas falls into a supermassive black hole; finding them early constrains how fast such black holes can grow
story.display_body: A quasar is a galaxy's core blazing as gas falls into a supermassive black hole; finding them early constrains how fast such black holes can grow. From about 18 months of Euclid wide-survey imaging, with follow-up at Keck, the Large Binocular Telescope, Hubble and JWST, the team places J1504+6252 (nicknamed Dún Aonghasa) at redshift 8.129 ± 0.005 — light emitted 630 million years after the Big Bang, when the universe was 5% of its present age. That is the first quasar known beyond redshift 8, and pushes the frontier back about 39 million years past Euclid's own previous record. JWST spectra give a black-hole mass of roughly 360 million Suns. Unusually it is feeding slowly now, so it must have grown in earlier, very rapid episodes. Masses from single spectra carry large uncertainties, and this is one object; Euclid's whole survey is expected to yield at most a few tens at this distance.
story.why: a 360-million-solar-mass black hole that is not currently gorging, seen this early, is hard to assemble in standard growth models, and it is the kind of object that decides between competing accounts of how the first black holes formed. Euclid is an ESA mission, and the discovery paper is led from ESO and MPIA in Germany.

story.headline: BepiColombo captured at Mercury after burn cut out
story.summary: The joint ESA–JAXA BepiColombo mission reached Mercury orbit on Saturday 21 November, the second spacecraft ever to do so after NASA's MESSENGER
story.display_body: The joint ESA–JAXA BepiColombo mission reached Mercury orbit on Saturday 21 November, the second spacecraft ever to do so after NASA's MESSENGER. ESA's own account is more complicated than arrival: the orbit-insertion burn, which started at 18:24 UTC, ended early, delivering about 77% of the planned change in velocity, and the spacecraft entered safe mode — the protective state it adopts when it meets conditions it does not expect. Controllers at ESOC in Darmstadt confirmed capture at about 01:00 local time, and have traced the fault, with Airbus, to a software issue in attitude guidance and thruster control. The resulting orbit has a 75-hour period instead of the planned 58 hours; the remaining burn sequence has been re-planned to absorb that, with no extra burns needed. The mission used "weak stability capture", arriving slowly enough for Mercury's gravity to hold it temporarily — previously used only at the Moon — which is why insertion takes a series of burns. Separation of the two science orbiters is still set for 9 December, with ESA's orbiter reaching its science orbit in March 2027 and observations starting that April.
story.why: reaching Mercury takes more energy than reaching the outer solar system, and this is only the second orbiter ever to manage it; eight years of cruise survived a failure on the final manoeuvre with the schedule intact.

story.headline: Milky Way's Norma arm may be the bar itself
story.summary: We cannot see our own galaxy from outside, so its shape is reconstructed from tracers inside it
story.display_body: We cannot see our own galaxy from outside, so its shape is reconstructed from tracers inside it. Masers — bright natural microwave beacons around young massive stars — have been used to trace a segment called the Norma arm, running from one end of the Milky Way's central bar. Using new N-body and hydrodynamic simulations, this Sydney-led team argues the million-year-old masers instead mark the shock front on the leading edge of the bar, equivalently its dust lane, where gas piles up as it crosses into the bar's orbit. That implies the dust lane is actively forming stars. Fitting the masers to the simulated shock front yields a bar that is long, slowly rotating and star-forming: semi-axes of about 4.3 and 2.3 kiloparsecs, inclined about 20°, with a pattern speed of at most 40 km/s per kiloparsec. It is an inference from simulations matched to tracers, not a direct measurement.
story.why: if one of the four arms in the standard picture of our galaxy is really part of the bar, both the Milky Way's spiral structure and the bar's disputed size and speed need revising — and the bar becomes a place where stars are born.

story.headline: Nature retracts gigaparsec anisotropy claim
story.summary: In June, Nature published a claim of anisotropic structures in the galaxy distribution on gigaparsec scales — a potential violation of the cosmological principle, the assumption that the universe looks statistically the same in every direction, on which modern cosmology rests
story.display_body: In June, Nature published a claim of anisotropic structures in the galaxy distribution on gigaparsec scales — a potential violation of the cosmological principle, the assumption that the universe looks statistically the same in every direction, on which modern cosmology rests. The authors have now retracted it, at the editors' suggestion. Shortly after publication Till Sawala identified the error: the analysis compared comoving distances between observed galaxies against luminosity distances between galaxies in the simulated comparison catalogues — two different distance measures. Correcting it drops the discrepancy to 1.48–2.75 sigma depending on how the sample is built, below cosmology's conventional 3-sigma bar. Both authors agree with the retraction, say their method remains valid as tentative evidence, and will submit a corrected version elsewhere.
story.why: the original claim was carried as a possible crack in the standard cosmological model, including in a daily brief here on 25 June. Five months later it is a 2-sigma hint, retracted — a reminder of how often an extraordinary cosmological signal turns out to be a mismatch between two definitions of distance.
